now.text: My work connects clinical sequence modelling, tools for scientific discovery, and research software. The common aim is to make complex evidence more useful for medical research.

sections.title: Clinical sequence modelling
sections.description: Understanding patterns in electronic health records and their value for medical research.

projects.title: ASCEND research arc
projects.summary: Modelling clinical trajectories to study risk, patterns of disease, and how clinical models can be interpreted.

projects.title: ORCA
projects.summary: Studying electronic health records as a language, with the aim of making clinical sequences easier to interpret and compare.

projects.title: Phenotype fingerprinting
projects.summary: Exploring how patterns in clinical records could help characterise under-recognised disease.

sections.title: Scientific discovery systems
sections.description: Making scientific literature and possible research directions easier to explore.

projects.title: NEXUS
projects.summary: Investigating where ideas and methods from one field might help solve problems in another.

projects.title: Physarum
projects.summary: Tools for comparing possible research directions and supporting scientific judgement.

projects.title: glucose.ai
projects.summary: A public literature-discovery site connecting diabetes research with developments in AI and machine learning.

sections.title: Research software
sections.description: Software that helps research remain connected and usable over time.

projects.title: pi / Cog workflows
projects.summary: Tools for connecting research sources, experiments and synthesis, so useful work is easier to organise and revisit.

milestones.title: Interpreting clinical sequence models
milestones.summary: A preprint on sparse autoencoder analysis of clinical sequence model representations is available on arXiv.

milestones.title: ASCENDgpt preprint
milestones.summary: A preprint on phenotype-aware cardiovascular risk prediction from electronic health records is available on arXiv.
